'''William "Vann" Parker''' (December 22, 1901 – November 25, 1987) was an American mathematician who worked primarily in [[Algebra|classical algebra]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Parker, William Vann |url=https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/author?authorId=514660 |website=MATHSCINET |publisher=American Mathematical Society |access-date=5 July 2025}}</ref> He was chair of the mathematics department at both [[Louisiana State University]] in the 1940s and [[Auburn University]] in the 1950s. He was also the Graduate Dean at Auburn during [[School integration in the United States|integration]] in Alabama.

== Early life and education ==
On December 22, 1901, Parker was born in [[Monroe, North Carolina]] to Benjamin Franklin Parker and Sarah Della Cox.<ref name="ua" /><ref name="PeopleLegacy">{{cite web |title=William Vann Parker |url=https://peoplelegacy.com/william_vann_parker-3L5806 |website=PeopleLegacy |access-date=5 July 2025}}</ref> He obtained a Bachelor of Arts degree from University of North Carolina in 1923<ref>{{cite news |title=Battle Appeals For World Court Before Carolina Graduates |url=https://newspapers.digitalnc.org/lccn/sn84020730/1923-06-14/ed-1/seq-5/ |access-date=5 July 2025 |agency=Durham morning herald. |issue=edition 1 |date=June 14, 1923}}</ref> followed by a Master of Arts degree the following year.<ref>{{cite web |title=One Hundred and Twenty-Ninth Annual Commencement The University of North Carolina |url=https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/07/Commencement_%281924%29_%28IA_commencement19241924univ%29.pdf |access-date=5 July 2025}}</ref> While at the University of North Carolina, he was a member of the Di Society, Math Club, Elisha Mitchell Scientific Society, and Union Country Club. He was also an Assistant Instructor in Mathematics during his senior year.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Howard |first1=Thomas Simmons |title=Yackety Yack |date=1923 |publisher=Dialectic and Philanthropic Literary Societies and the Fraternities of The University of North Carolina Chapel Hill N.C. |page=107 |edition=33 |url=https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e6/Yackety_yack_%28serial%29_%28IA_yacketyyackseria1923univ%29.pdf |access-date=5 July 2025}}</ref> He attended [[Princeton University]] between 1926 and 1927; and eventually obtain a PhD at [[Brown University]] in 1931 under his advisor [[Albert Arnold Bennett Jr.|Albert Arnold Bennett]].<ref name="ua">{{cite web |title=PARKER, WILLIAM VANN, 1901-1987 |url=https://www.lib.ua.edu/Alabama_Authors/?p=1858 |website=Alabama Authors |access-date=3 July 2025}}</ref><ref name="Plainsman" />

== Career ==
In 1924, he began teaching at the University of the South until 1925. He would then teach at the [[University of North Carolina]] between 1925 and 1931. During his attendance at Princeton University he taught there as well. In 1931, he started teaching at [[Mississippi Woman's College]] until 1934. He then started teaching at [[Georgia Tech|Georgia Institute of Technology]] in 1934 until 1936 where he was one of the first people hired there to have a doctorate degree.<ref name="GIT" /> In 1936, he became an associate professor at [[Louisiana State University]] where he advised Anthony Aucoin (1940) and John Currie (1948).<ref name="MGP">{{cite web |title=William Vann Parker |url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=4284 |website=Mathematics Genealogy Project |access-date=3 July 2025}}</ref><ref name="GIT">{{cite web |last1=Duke |first1=Richard |title=Mathematics at Georgia Tech: The First Hundred Years, 1888 1987 |url=https://math.gatech.edu/sites/default/files/documents/georgiatech-school-of-math-history_1.pdf |department=School of Mathematics |website=Georgia Institute of Technology |access-date=3 July 2025}}</ref> In 1943, he would become the head of the math department at Louisiana State University until leaving in 1947. He then became a regents professor at [[University of Georgia]] between 1947 and 1950.<ref name="1988Alumni">{{cite web |title=The University Report March 1988 |url=https://www.carolinaalumnireview.com/carolinaalumnireview/ur198803/MobilePagedReplica.action?pm=2&folio=34#pg34 |website=Carolina Alumni Review |access-date=5 July 2025}}</ref><ref name="Plainsman" />

===Years at Auburn===
In 1950 he became the head of the mathematics department at [[Auburn University|Alabama Polytechnic Institute]], now known as Auburn University, a role he would hold until 1965.<ref>{{Cite web |title=History of Mathematics at UGA {{!}} Department of Mathematics |url=https://www.math.uga.edu/history-mathematics-uga |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=www.math.uga.edu}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Glomerata |date=2004 |page=92 |edition=107 |url=https://content.lib.auburn.edu/digital/collection/gloms2004/id/6132 |access-date=5 July 2025}}</ref> He is credited for creating the mathematics program at Auburn.<ref name="cosam">{{cite web |title=History of COSAM |url=https://www.auburn.edu/cosam/about/history.htm |department=College of Sciences and Mathematics |website=Auburn University |access-date=3 July 2025}}</ref> In 1953, he took on the additional role of Graduate Dean at Auburn until his retirement on July 1, 1972.<ref name="Alumni1972">{{cite news |title=Class Notes 23'-50th Reunion 1973 |url=https://www.carolinaalumnireview.com/carolinaalumnireview/ur197210/MobilePagedReplica.action?pm=2&folio=12#pg12 |access-date=5 July 2025 |agency=The University Report |date=October 1972}}</ref> From 1953 to 1971 he was a council representative of Auburn University for the [[Oak Ridge Associated Universities]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Pollard |first1=William G. |title=ORAU: From the Beginning |date=1980 |publisher=Oak Ridge Associated Universities |isbn=0930780043 |page=135 |url=https://orau.org/about/book/orau-from-the-beginning.pdf |access-date=5 July 2025}}</ref> At Auburn he advised, Robert Ackerson (1955) and Marion Wicht Sr. (1957).<ref name="MGP" /> As head of the Math Department in 1960, he traveled to near [[Washington, D.C.]] to interviewed [[Emilie Virginia Haynsworth|Emillie Haynsworth]] by having her work on a research problem with him in matrix theory until the end of his trip when he stated that she could have a job at Auburn.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Carlson |first1=David |title=Emilie Haynsworth, 1916–1985 |journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications |date=March 1986 |volume=75 |pages=269–276 |doi=10.1016/0024-3795(86)90194-1 |url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0024-3795%2886%2990194-1 |access-date=4 July 2025|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

While he was the dean of the graduate school he oversaw the first doctorate programs at Auburn. As dean of the graduate school, he was the defendant in the court case Franklin v. Parker. Parker rejected [[Harold Franklin]]'s application to the graduate school at Auburn for not graduating from a college that was accredited with the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools. The court found that this is a reasonable policy in an ideal world. However, given that Alabama only accredited the white schools and let the black schools accreditations to expire, Parker was found to have discriminated against Franklin by following the policy that he was instructed to follow.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Johnson |first1=Frank Minis |title=Franklin v. Parker |url=https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2261143/franklin-v-parker/ |website=Court Listener |access-date=5 July 2025}}</ref> In January 1964, Parker and Malcolm McMillan, a history professor, helped Franklin register for classes at the library while the [[National Guard (United States)|national guard]] ensured their safety from the crowds.<ref>{{Cite news |date=January 5, 1964 |title=AUBURN U. CALM AS NEGRO ENTERS; Troopers Provide Protection at School in Alabama |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/01/05/archives/auburn-u-calm-as-negro-enters-troopers-provide-protection-at-school.html |access-date=December 13, 2025 |work=New York Times}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==

He was a member of the [[Mathematics Association of America]]. He helped start the Alabama Association of College Teachers of Mathematics.<ref name="ua">{{cite web |title=PARKER, WILLIAM VANN, 1901-1987 |url=https://www.lib.ua.edu/Alabama_Authors/?p=1858 |website=Alabama Authors |access-date=3 July 2025}}</ref> He was a member of [[Sigma Xi]] and [[Pi Mu Epsilon]].<ref name="Plainsman">{{cite news |title=the Auburn Plainsman |url=https://content.lib.auburn.edu/digital/collection/plainsman/id/1243/rec/1369 |access-date=3 August 2025 |work=content.lib.auburn.edu |agency=Alabama Polytechnic Institute |volume=LXXVI |issue=14 |date=January 11, 1950 |language=en}}</ref>

He was listed in Who's Who in America for 1976–1977.<ref name="ua" /><ref name="parker">{{cite web |title=WILLIAM VANN PARKER |url=https://www.lib.auburn.edu/ladc/buildings/images/parker.jpg |access-date=3 July 2025}}</ref> He was also included in Who's Who in the South and Southwest, Who's Who Education, Who's Who Atoms, American Men of Science, and Leaders in American Science.<ref name="parker" />

== Personal life ==

He married the genealogist and writer Carolyn Adele Edwards on July 3, 1926.<ref name="ua" /><ref name="1988Alumni" /> In February 1960, Carolyn became a member of the [[United Daughters of the Confederacy]], [[Raphael Semmes|Admiral Semmes]] Chapter in Auburn, Al.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://content.lib.auburn.edu/digital/api/collection/testfa/id/2460/download |title=Finding Aid - Inventory Auburn University – Special Collections and Archives Collection Name: United Daughters of the Confederacy, Admiral Semmes Chapter, Auburn, Alabama |date=14 October 2008}}</ref> Carolyn and Vann Parker had a son and two daughters.<ref name="1988Alumni" /> For more than 60 years, he was a part of the [[Masonic lodge|University Masonic Lodge at Chapel Hill]].<ref name="1988Alumni" />

His daughter Emily "Anne" Parker Battle followed in his footsteps studying mathematics and then teaching mathematics at the [[University of Alabama at Birmingham]] and the [[University of Montevallo]].<ref>{{cite web |title=OBITUARY Emily Anne Battle |url=https://www.dignitymemorial.com/obituaries/montevallo-al/emily-battle-7550585 |website=Dignity Memorial |access-date=5 July 2025}}</ref>

== Death and legacy ==
In his honor, the Auburn Board of Trustees decided to name the mathematics building Parker Hall.<ref name="ua" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Sutton |first=Amber |date=2016-06-03 |title=Samford, Haley and Jordan-Hare: Explaining 31 Auburn University namesakes |url=https://www.al.com/living/2016/06/auburn_buildings.html |access-date=2026-04-15 |website=al |language=en}}</ref> Parker died on November 25, 1987, in Birmingham, Alabama, and was buried at Auburn Memorial Park Cemetery.<ref name="1988Alumni" /><ref name="PeopleLegacy" /> The Alabama Association of College Teachers of Mathematics holds a lecture named after Parker and [[Fred A. Lewis]] of the University of Alabama at their annual meeting called the "Lewis-Parker Lecture" to honor a mathematician from the state of [[Alabama]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Lewis Parker Lectures – AACTM |url=https://www.ajmonline.org/aactm/lewis-parker-lectures/ |access-date=2025-08-03 |language=en-US}}</ref>
